title: How to Make Custom-Length Christmas Light Runs with Empty Socket Wire
metaTitle: Custom Length Christmas Light Runs | Holiday Lights Direct
metaDescription: How to build custom-length C9 Christmas light runs with empty socket wire and vampire plugs, with bulb limits and testing, for Canadian homes and installers.
excerpt: A practical walkthrough of measuring, cutting and terminating C7/C9 empty socket wire with male and female vampire plugs, fitting the bulbs, testing on the ground, and knowing how many bulbs one run can carry before you start another.
heroAlt: Installer cutting green C9 empty socket wire to length on a driveway and fitting an SPT-2 male vampire plug before hanging a custom Christmas light run on an Ontario home
keyTakeaways: Custom runs are built from three parts: empty socket wire with sockets every 12 inches, plain SPT-2 wire for the unlit stretches, and male and female vampire plugs that pierce the cord without stripping.
Measure the roofline first, plan where the unlit sections fall, then cut the socket wire between sockets so every cut end has a clean tail for the plug.
The male plug goes at the power end and the female plug at the far end, so runs can be joined in series and no bare cord is left exposed.
Count sockets, not feet: at 12 inch spacing a 100 ft section carries roughly 100 bulbs, and the total wattage on the line decides when to start a new run.
Test every run flat on the ground before it goes on a ladder, and label the male end with its location so next year's install takes minutes instead of hours.

body.text: Pre-made light strings come in the lengths the factory chose, which is never the length of your roofline. Professional installers stopped fighting that years ago. They buy empty socket wire on a spool, cut it to the exact run they need, snap a plug on each end and fill it with the bulbs the customer picked. The result fits the house with no dark gap at the corner and no bundle of leftover bulbs stuffed behind the downspout. This guide walks through the whole process with the C7/C9 empty socket wire, SPT-2 plain wire, vampire plugs and faceted C9 LED bulbs sold by Holiday Lights Direct, for homeowners and crews alike. The same runs go back up in the same places every year, and a damaged socket or section is swapped or cut out and rejoined rather than replacing a whole string.
What you need

items: C7/C9 empty socket wire with 12 inch socket spacing, on a 120 ft or 1000 ft spool, in green or white. C9 sockets are E17 base; C7 sockets are E12 base.
Plain SPT-2 18 AWG wire in the matching colour, 250 ft or 500 ft, for the lead from the outlet and any unlit jumpers.
SPT-2 male and female vampire plugs. Buy a few more than the number of runs you plan, because one will be clamped crooked at some point.
Faceted C9 LED bulbs in the colour or colours you want. Packs of 25 suit a single home; packs of 500 are the installer size.
A tape measure or a measuring wheel for long rooflines and parapets.
Sharp side cutters or wire snips. A clean, square cut matters for the plug to seat.
A permanent marker and a roll of tape for labelling each run.
An outlet, an extension cord or a plug-in outlet tester for ground-level testing.
Work gloves, a stable ladder or lift, and a helper for anything above a single storey.

body.text: Never cut, plug or unplug a line that is connected to power. Build and test everything on the ground, then unplug it before it goes up. Roofline work belongs on a dry day above freezing whenever the calendar allows.
Step by step
1. Measure the roofline, not the wire

Walk the house with a tape and note the length of every section you want lit: each eave, each gable, each ridge if you are doing one. Note the corners and where the run will turn. Then note the location of the outlet, because that decides where the lead starts and how long it must be. A sketch on the back of an envelope is enough, but write the numbers down. Guessing from the ground is how people end up with 90 ft of bulbs on a 100 ft eave.
2. Plan the unlit sections

Decide where you do not want bulbs: across a garage door, over a picture window, down the fascia to the outlet, or across a gap between two roof sections. Those stretches get plain SPT-2 wire instead of socket wire. Each transition from lit to unlit needs a plug pair, a female plug on the end of one section and a male plug on the start of the next, so count those transitions and add them to your plug order.
3. Cut the socket wire between sockets

Unroll the socket wire along a driveway or a garage floor rather than cutting from the spool in the air. Measure your first section, find the socket nearest the length you need, and cut the cord in the middle of the gap between that socket and the next one. That leaves roughly six inches of cord past the last socket at each end, which is what the plug needs. Make the cut square, straight across both conductors. A diagonal cut leaves one conductor short and the plug teeth may miss it.
4. Fit the male plug at the power end

Open the vampire plug and look at the channel: it is shaped for the flat SPT-2 cord to sit one way. Most plugs are marked on the body to show which conductor goes to which blade. SPT cord has one conductor with a ribbed or ridged jacket and one that is smooth, and the ribbed conductor is the identified conductor that pairs with the wider blade on a polarised plug. Follow the moulded marking on the plug body, lay the cord fully into the channel so the end is against the stop, and close the cover firmly until the teeth pierce the jacket and the cover latches. Do not split the two conductors apart for a vampire plug; it is designed to bite through the intact cord.
5. Fit the female plug at the far end

The female plug is fitted the same way on the other end. It does two jobs. It seals the cut end so no bare copper is exposed to weather, and it lets you plug the next run in without a splice. Even if this is the last run on the house and nothing will ever be plugged into it, fit a female plug rather than leaving the tail taped: a taped end is where corrosion starts and where a curious child or a squirrel finds live copper. Plain-wire jumpers for the unlit stretches, and the lead from the outlet, are built the same way: a length of SPT-2 with a male plug on one end and a female on the other, cut slightly long so it drops into the clip line without pulling the socket wire tight around a corner.
6. Insert the bulbs

Screw a C9 LED bulb into each E17 socket until it is snug. The faceted lens should sit straight in the socket; if one is leaning, back it out and re-seat it rather than forcing it. Fill every socket, including the ones that will sit behind a downspout, because an empty socket is an open socket in the weather. For colour patterns, lay the bulbs out on the ground first; it is easier to change your mind on the driveway than on the roof.
7. Test on the ground before it goes up

Plug the finished run into the outlet or a tester with the whole run laid out flat. Every bulb should light. A dark bulb usually means it is not fully seated; a dark run means a plug was fitted with the cord not pushed fully into the channel. Fix it now, unplug, then coil the run loosely starting from the female end so the male plug is on the outside of the coil and ready to go up first. Write the location on a strip of tape at the male end: front eave left, garage gable, and so on.
Socket spacing and what it means for your count

The empty socket wire has a socket every 12 inches, so the number of bulbs on a run is the number of feet, give or take one at each cut. A 40 ft eave takes about 40 bulbs; a full 120 ft spool cut into a single run takes about 120. This is the spacing most rooflines look best at with C9 bulbs, dense enough to read as a continuous line from the street without the bulbs crowding each other. For tighter detail on short railings or window frames, C7 bulbs on the same 12 inch line look lighter.
How many bulbs per run

The honest answer is that it depends on the bulbs, the wire and what feeds it. Add up the watts of every bulb on the run and divide by 120 to get the current in amps. Compare that against the rating printed on the plug and on the wire, and keep a healthy margin below the lowest of them. Then look at the circuit: a standard household outlet is fed by a breaker shared with other loads, and every run you daisy-chain into the same outlet adds to it.

items: Faceted C9 LED bulbs draw a small fraction of the power of an incandescent, so on LED the wire and plug ratings allow a long run. Check the bulb wattage on the product page and do the math for your own count.
Incandescent C9 bulbs are commonly rated around 7 watts each, so 100 of them already sit near 700 watts and close to 6 amps. Incandescent runs must be kept short and never daisy-chained casually.
SPT-2 18 AWG is commonly rated at 10 amps in the trade, but treat the figure printed on your wire and plug as the authority and stay well under it.
Leave room on the breaker for the inflatable, the wreath and whatever else the household plugs in outside in December.

body.text: When to start a new run

items: When the wattage math gets close to the wire or plug rating. Split the roofline into two runs fed from opposite ends, or from a second outlet.
At every unlit gap. A separate run each side of a garage door with a plain-wire jumper between them is easier to hang and easier to repair than one long piece with a dead section.
Wherever the run would exceed what one person can carry up a ladder in a coil. Around 100 ft of socket wire with bulbs is a comfortable single-person handful.
When the colour changes. Keeping one colour per run makes next year's re-hang and any bulb replacement much simpler.

body.text: Common mistakes and how to avoid them

items: Cutting through a socket instead of between sockets. Always cut in the middle of the gap so the plug has a tail to grip.
Using the wrong plug for the wire. SPT-2 plugs go on SPT-2 cord. A plug that closes with no resistance is on wire that is too thin.
Pushing the cord only part-way into the plug channel. If the end is not against the stop, one tooth can miss its conductor and the run is dead or intermittent.
Leaving an unplugged, untaped tail on the last run. Fit a female plug.
Mixing LED and incandescent bulbs on the same run. Keep the load math simple by keeping the bulb types separate.

body.text: Once the runs are built, labelled and tested, hanging them is the quick part, and the same runs go back up in the same places next season with no measuring at all. faq.q: Where exactly do I cut empty socket wire?
faq.a: In the middle of the gap between two sockets, straight across both conductors. That leaves a clean tail of a few inches beyond the last socket at each end for the vampire plug to grip.

faq.q: Which plug goes on which end of the run?
faq.a: The male plug goes at the end nearest the power source and the female plug at the far end. That lets you join runs in series and leaves no bare copper exposed, even on the last run.

faq.q: How many C9 bulbs can I put on one run?
faq.a: Add up the watts of every bulb and divide by 120 for amps, then stay well under the lowest rating printed on the wire and plug. Faceted LED C9s allow long runs; incandescent C9s at around 7 watts each must be kept much shorter. Check the bulb wattage on the product page.

faq.q: Do I have to strip the wire to fit a vampire plug?
faq.a: No. Vampire plugs have teeth that pierce the jacket of the intact SPT-2 cord when the cover is closed. Lay the cord fully into the channel against the stop, follow the marking for the ribbed conductor, and press the cover until it latches.

faq.q: Can I fit C7 bulbs to C9 socket wire?
faq.a: No. C9 sockets are E17 base and C7 sockets are E12 base, and the bulbs are not interchangeable. Buy the socket wire that matches the bulb size you intend to use, and use replacement E17 or E12 sockets of the same type for repairs.
